text:
When you type a web address into your browser, a lookup called DNS resolution turns that name into the numeric IP address computers use to find each other. The browser first checks its own cache to see whether it has looked up the domain recently. If it has a saved answer, it uses that and skips the remaining steps. If not, the request goes to a recursive resolver, which is a server usually run by your internet provider or by a public DNS service.

The resolver works through the naming hierarchy one level at a time. It starts with a root server, which points it to the right top-level domain (TLD) server, such as the one for ".com". The TLD server sends the resolver to the authoritative server for that domain, and the authoritative server returns the IP address. The resolver passes the answer back to your browser. Both of them cache it for a set period called the time to live (TTL), which is typically 300 seconds, or five minutes. A TTL that short means repeat visits load quickly, and if the address changes, the new one spreads soon afterward.
